#3767. How Origame Digital are channelling and defacing Lovecraft over a trilogy of "inherently indigenous" anti-fascist games

Revisiting the secretive design of Penguin Colony

Much like the H.P. Lovecraft novella it alternately riffs on and skewers, Penguin Colony takes you to an ancient alien city of crabby cuboid geometry and helical designs – comparable at a glance to Lovecraft's "terraces of every sort of provocative disproportion", but here given strangely everyday, anachronistic-seeming labels, such as "Downtown". Later, you're shown flashes of footage of the streets of Melbourne in Australia - developer Origame Digital's base of operations, and a city built on stolen Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung and Bunurong Boon Wurrung land.

When I first set foot in Downtown, in the unassuming body of a Rockhopper penguin, I thought the broad idea was to satirically redefine modern settlements built by European colonisers as Lovecraftian relics, intrusions from the cosmic beyond. This irony seems most pointed in sections where you steer a group of Māori characters, journeying south to prevent an expedition of German and British Nazi occultists from resurrecting a surviving elder being they call the "one true Aryan king". Playing as one of the Māori voyagers, you witness the cyclopean city as a realm of spectral high rises and square windows, rearing out of a swamp of blood and bone.

I'm only somewhat correct about all this. Penguin Colony's reference points are wide-ranging and precise, with the persona of a disinterested penguin serving partly as a means of critical distance from Lovecraft, and partly, as a kind of camouflage for an extremely complex political artwork. It's easy to treat the game's critique as wholly retrospective - an alternately mocking and outraged investigation of a horror author whose bigotry is often reduced to an apologetic footnote or tinny performative disclaimer, drowned out by dread augurs of tentacles in the dark. It's a test of interpretative rigour, amongst other things, for hasty white European reviewers who might slip and slide past the more elaborate allusions into idle chat about Soulslikes.

Speaking to me over videocall, Origame Digital founder and director Naphtali Faulkner acknowledged the broad objective of reframing colonial cities as unearthly aberrations, cutting against cosier visions of colonised Australian land. "There's a bit of an issue with Australian games, where they tend to be tourism pieces, sometimes," he comments. "Not in a bad way, but they do not bring up the violence of this country, in anything. They will comfortably sidestep that for a lot of reasons – one is, a lot of the families that are affected by that are still around. Is it [a non-indigenous developer's] place to tell that story? No. But also, you have this sort of 'Australiana' stuff happen quite a lot, where it's tin roofs and red dirt, that kind of look you see on a postcard."

Still, Penguin Colony's "first colonial city" isn't just a response to 'Australiana'. It's also a monument to 2b2t, the ancient Minecraft "anarchy" server that is infamous for its vicious player culture, and somewhat admired for the colossal strangeness of its desecrated geography. 2b2t is an incarnation of Mojang's sandbox building sim that is so 'pure' and unsparing in its priorities that license owners Microsoft can't entirely acknowledge it. The server's central spawn has been repeatedly built up, defaced and degraded over 16 years of constant operation, forming a nightmare landscape of lavafalls and Wither holes and floating seas and basalt barricades.

"We took data from that, and we modified it, and made it playable," Faulkner tells me. "We had to subdivide it, and it had more detail and stuff, and really transform it a lot, but the whole thing was: what is 2b2t? It's the most realistic depiction of colonisation in a videogame. When you do Minecraft, it's basically a colonisation simulator where you go extract the trees and stuff but it all magically regrows. 2b2t's only rules are there's no rules, and also nothing respawns. You have the Spawn - the Spawn is the most heart-wrenching thing to look at when you first see it, because you know what Minecraft is in your head, you've seen those rolling green hills, and then to see it basically be destroyed into oblivion, is a very strong emotion."

As an inadvertent digital document of colonialism, 2b2t doesn't offer much hope of reparation and redress. "The only way to build back the Spawn is to go back and replant everything," Faulkner says. "And you know, fix the damage that was done, but we all know what gamers did to it, right? They've done various incursions and things like covering it in lava or water, or making it so that you can't leave without cheats." Still, Faulkner considers it "a fascinating relic of gaming". In general, he is interested in how fiction makers might preserve virtual landscapes that reflect "player-run digital ecosystems of people basically going beyond what the designers thought."

2b2t's presence within Penguin Colony is illustrative of how Origame Digital are using Lovecraft over the course of a planned trilogy of "inherently indigenous" Lovecraftian games – not just rebutting the author's anglophilia and white supremacism, not merely flipping the racial power dynamics so as to "make the indigenous people the skull-measuring scientists", but taking Lovecraft's mythos to unfamiliar places and forcing it to serve a politics that Lovecraft himself would despise.

Faulkner himself came across Lovecraft's work around 15 years ago, having been introduced to it by a university friend. He was unmoved, initially, by the author's descriptions of eldritch threats and incomprehensible dimensions. "You know how Lovecraft's described, with Cthulhu - 'unknowable horror', 'madness inducing'," he says. "And then you see it and it's kind of like an octopus. It's a bit underwhelming." Faulkner grew more intrigued by Lovecraft, however, after seeing other artists adapt his work. He points to the Shadows Over Innsmouth music video created by Carpenter Brut - a contributor to Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's OST - and also, to Victor LaValle's The Ballad of Black Tom, an adaptation of Lovecraft's The Horror at Red Hook written from the perspective of a Black man. "I started to understand that Lovecraft isn't just the author's works," he says. "It's this all-encompassing thing that has inspired so much stuff."

Even as he pondered Lovecraft and the broader, somewhat dissociative genre of the Lovecraftian, Faulkner was also investigating his own heritage as a Ngāi Te Rangi person living in a former British colony, tracing patterns of invasion, conquest and assimilation that, he says, have repeated themselves since the days of the Romans and Vikings. "I think the reason that I decided to do this, was that when I started to get Lovecraft, it was when I was really starting to have the understanding that every indigenous person has at some point about what colonisation is," he says. "You know, where you have to learn your own family history, and you have to learn why things are the way they are at the moment. And so to me, it was like that thing of, when you start seeing Lovecraft as this thing about displacement, invasion, destruction, language - it reached me at the perfect time in my life when I was already looking at this stuff, and I thought that it was a really apt analogy."

Faulkner also sensed that even Lovecraft enthusiasts who are less mindful of the author's politics were yearning for a fresher kind of Lovecraftian fable. "When it comes to indigenous stuff, the thing is that we're not really represented in anything, and our histories are rarely given a platform to say stuff, especially in games," he goes on. "But what I'd sort of looked at with Lovecraft, was that I think fans were ready for it, because people had gotten a little tired of these direct, 1-to-1 adaptations, that still exist in the space of the unknowable horror is unknowable, rather than trying to say, why is the unknowable horror scary?"

The idea of the "unknowable" pervades Lovecraftian fiction, as does the idea of "cosmic indifference", that terror of being engulfed in a vaster universe of forms and forces that barely register the existence of human beings. This "unknowability" is concentrated in the balefully blank gaze of Psurumin, the otherworldly entity at the far end of Penguin Colony - the last Earthly remnant of an empire spanning hundreds of planets. "I stare into its eyes," intones Howard Blakely, the game's English narrator, and an initially unconsenting member of the doomed Nazi expedition. "I stare deep within, and yet I see nothing. I am not even a speck of inane curiosity."

Penguin Colony overlaps this Lovecraftian "cosmic indifference" with Faulkner's grief and bewilderment at how perpetrators of empire have insulated themselves from feelings of responsibility or shame. "For example in the southern hemisphere here, Australia and New Zealand, the idea was that the missionaries would say 'don't worry, we're saving them, we're turning them into Christians, we had to kill the ones who resist'," he says. "And the soldiers that had immense trauma and guilt from doing that would be consulted by a priest and told, 'you were doing it for the greater good'."

"To me it's saying: how could they do that to us?" Faulkner goes on. "What made them do that? To me as a younger person, it was very 'unknowable'. You've probably talked to other indigenous people, I hope, before in your life, and it's this kind of thing especially where there's a lot of pain there, because... how could someone choose to do that? And even to this day, there's a question around even saying sorry about it. Or there's questions around people, they want to sort of move on from history, and never bring it up, never acknowledge it again, whilst the injustice of colonisation is still present."

Howard Blakely is a mirror of sorts for this culture of denial and obfuscation. For all his apparent awareness that Psurumin does not regard him as a fellow being, and that to release the creature would be calamitous, he succumbs to the idea that he can ship the starspawn home as yet another trophy for the British Empire. He dreams of being honoured as a great pioneer by "the London School of Eugenics", and retiring to a cottage in Western Victoria. These reflections are accompanied by archive illustrations of colonial officers storming the frontier, and video snapshots of Psurumin statues in Melbourne's civic centres.

Blakely is similarly befuddled about his German Nazi hosts, who are initially his captors. While cautious of them, he also doesn't see the Nazis as altogether bad. After all, some of them are fellow scholars – surely, they are too refined, too cultured, to be altogether irredeemable. "He doesn't see himself in history, as he walks through this place," Faulkner comments. "He doesn't see the Nazis as the people that we see them as." In this, Blakely echoes Dyer, narrator of Lovecraft's At The Mountain Of Madness, who comes to admire the star-faring colonisers his team unearth in the far south, calling them "men of another age and another order of being". But he is also an expression of political myopia and creeping fascism in the present.

The inspiration for Blakely came partly from Faulkner's own time in the academic world. "There are tonnes of people who are scientists first, and political thinkers 17th in their thoughts," he comments, recalling his encounters with Trump supporters as a student. "People who don't consider themselves political and then end up taking incredible political stances on stuff, until it becomes clear that they do actually have a political ideology, that's sort of formed by being around the people they're around." Faulkner's other reference points for Blakely include Elon Musk, once "washed through the media as a green, eco-warrior guy", latterly an advocate for 'great replacement' theories and far-right uprisings.

Faulkner says that Penguin Colony's anti-fascist sentiments are especially aimed at "the rise of gen-Z fascism", expressed in online transphobia and anti-Semitic memes. "There's been a huge uptick in people trying to vindicate Hitler, and trying to rehabilitate him in the eyes of this young generation," he says. "What they say is things like 'the painter was right'." Faulkner thinks that this neofascism has "petered out a little bit" over the past ten years, but is still on the march. Above all, he sees its resurgence in the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, and in the qualms many self-described anti-fascists have about condemning it.

"I and every indigenous person I know, in and out of the games industry, have no nuanced emotions about what is happening there," Faulkner continues. "We know what this is. Like, it's our family stories come to life. We can see what this was. We're not just hearing stories anymore. And we're not just noticing the violence happening to the indigenous people right now. We're noticing how the mostly white, non-indigenous people are still conflicted on it and confused on it, and they don't have clarity on this. The idea with this game was to really bring this into focus, because the games industry likes to say that indigenous people are welcome. And they want to welcome us at our events. What does that mean? You guys want us here to talk, but you're not going to acknowledge the genocide of indigenous people that's happening in front of you, that every single human being at this point knows about."

Penguin Colony ends with a statement calling out the games industry at large for holding its collective tongue about the Israeli military's brutal campaign, noting that such "cowardice" will be "recorded by the art that it makes". The flipside of that sentiment is that art can be a record of courage and principle, advancing and nourishing a culture in which xenophobia and colonial ideology are unable to thrive. I see this idea expressed, again, in the journey of the Māori group, who are equipped to prevent Psurumin's return because they have made doing so a tradition and a practice.

"They know from generations of story, that you have to do it," says Faulkner. "That it's a responsibility to do it, when it happens." Thwarting Psurumin is part of the Māori's creative lifework, part of their journey together. "It is the job of our descendants to carry forward the story of our resistance," intones one of their group, the game's second narrator. "To create song, dance and story, so our people move toward the light and away from darkness... Every 100 years, to compose new haka and follow new paths unknown to our enemy."

As a whole, Penguin Colony aims to be one such path away from darkness, its methods a mixture of bald and oblique, overt and covert. I have barely broken the surface in this piece. There's an angry hopefulness to the game that coexists with the spectacle of a distinctly 'double-A' penguin bumping and slithering along boulevards of blue-toned, recessed stone. The player is invited to participate in that hope by the game's closing "expedition" screens, which present all the lore you've gathered – including photographs taken by the Nazis, and textual fragments of devious origin – as a web of stars, floating over an illustration of the Zodiac.

The invocation of constellations is gently subversive because a constellation is an act of selective reading, stringing together sparks in a void. Treat the lore as something you can individually exhaust or "100%", as in many RPGs, and your selective reading will vanish into the mass of motes. Rather than 'completing' the star map in solitude, the game invites players to reach out to each other and compare their constellations – a homage to a "pre-social media" era when the distribution of information was less the province of monolithic digital platforms, and also, a framework for political solidarity. "As we live in a world which continues to push us further apart, we invite you to come together, talk, share, and interpret what you saw," the game suggests.

The call isn't open to all, however. Penguin Colony is consciously designed to repel those who might identify with its Nazis, appropriating the portrayal much as alt-right memesters sought to deify Anakin Skywalker, in the run-up to this year's US midterms. As a rhetorical apparatus, Penguin Colony is full of traps, easily overlooked if you focus on its headline politics. "We have a character voiced by a German trans woman – they can't enjoy it," notes Faulkner. "It just makes their skin crawl." There are many more such snares in the game. The commentary on Israel and Palestine, especially, pervades Penguin Colony in ways I don't think any player has yet discovered.

The lore of Penguin Colony also harbours clues about Origame's future "inherently indigenous" Lovecraftian games. The next game in that trilogy was actually conceived before Penguin Colony, and will be set decades from now. Faulkner envisages it as a loose retelling of Shadows Over Innsmouth, Lovecraft's story about fishpeople cults and miscegenation in a remote coastal town. "It's this idea of, what does Lovecraft look like in a future that we're heading towards, in the sense of social isolation and landscapes of small town decay."

In place of a Dagon cult, Origame Digital's next game will focus on groups of secretive violent bigots, with the player playing the part of a detective - a premise that, more superficially, makes me eager for a resurrection of the photography mechanics in Origame's reputation-making Umurangi Generation. As with Penguin Colony, the concept draws heavily on Faulkner's own life experiences.

"I grew up in a cattle town, and cattle towns are notoriously pretty racist places," he says. "The whole thing is when I left the town, when I was 18, just because I was going to university, I learned that the town had an active KKK [branch] that was being run out of the Anglican church. And this town is one town away from Grafton, which is where the white supremacist terrorist Brenton Tarrant is from – the guy who went and shot up the mosque in Christchurch. How does that happen? Where everyone knows about it, but they hush up?" The forthcoming game will look at how bitterness and neglect may give rise to such hatred, as local economies dry up and support structures are stripped away.

The second game will also take inspiration from the North American concept of a "sundown town", in which non-white people face violence if they linger outdoors after sunset - a vicious history also explored in Matt Ruff's HBO-adapted novel Lovecraft Country. "I went through a big rabbit hole on Youtube of hearing stories of people talking about, like, getting lost on the highway, needing to stop for gas, and then realising they had to stop it for gas at a sundown town," Faulkner explains. "They stopped there. They go to pay. And the clerk just sort of gives them a look, and then nudges over to them that there's a guy in the back of the shop just looking at them. And then suddenly they're followed on the highway for an hour."

The final game in Origame Digital's planned trilogy is far more formless, right now, but Faulkner has dreams of venturing into the realm of cooperative multiplayer. "It's not even written down on paper yet," he says. "We've just talked about it. For one thing, I don't know if I've got the skills to do it, because Penguin Colony had some jank, and had some technical issues at launch, but I'm getting better at making games."

This multiplayer project would build on Penguin Colony's premise of playing a colony, hopping between penguin bodies while shadowing Blakely's expedition. It would also follow through on the former game's closing encouragement to make allies against inhumanity via the collective interpretation of a celestial expanse of lore. "It's about the whole group, and I think if the third one was going to make a point about coming together to solve the problem… you probably want to make that a mechanical issue," Faulkner speculates, "where we have to actually make players do these sorts of actions together."

#3766. "Something's really possible" - Mass Effect cast rally around efforts to save the franchise on the first N7 Day after BioWare's closure

I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'"

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

"A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that company from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.

Pioner seemed headed in the right direction when it went into early access in late 2025, but it all went wrong just a few months later.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Pioner, a survival-shooter we said looked like "Stalker and Tarkov's alien baby" when we first laid eyes on it in 2021, is ending development and closing down. In an announcement posted today on Steam, developer GFAGames said further work on the game and continued operation of its servers requires more money, and it just doesn't have any.

"Over the past few months, we have been in talks with existing and potential partners about investment and new ways of working together that would allow us to preserve the project and the team," the studio wrote.

"We were unable to agree on the funding needed to continue the project. The studio no longer has sufficient funds of its own to continue development and keep the servers running."

Pioner looked promising when it turned up at the PC Gaming Show in 2021: A mash-up of Stalker, Metro, and Escape From Tarkov that featured both a singleplayer campaign and online co-op and PvP survival action, all of it built around late Soviet-era technology.

It launched into early access in December 2025 and worked its way to a peak concurrent player count of 1,686 on Steam a few months later—not huge, but far from catastrophic, and trending in the right direction.

Those numbers tailed off badly over the summer, though, as the dev team struggled with technical issues and updates came at a much slower pace than promised. August saw player counts collapse almost completely, and by mid-September only a couple dozen people were still playing.

Numerous replies to the shutdown announcement call for refunds to be issued, but GFAGames hasn't commented on those demands at this point. It also hasn't said when the game will actually be taken offline—I've reached out to ask and will update if I receive a reply.

The comedian finally addressed the controversy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Shane Gillis has been under fire recently for comments he made during his SNL monologue. The comedian, who has hosted multiple episodes of the NBC mainstay despite his complicated history with the show, told a joke about the way women dress when they go to the gym. It used a word to describe women that many took umbrage at. Now, the comic is opening up about how he felt in the aftermath of the controversy, and how he actually feels about the topic.

For context, during the October 10th episode of SNL, Gillis joked about returning to the gym after a long absence. The comedian noted that he didn't realize women were wearing such provocative outfits to the fitness center, and even called them “whores.” People were so upset, they forgot he also dropped an F-Bomb that night. The word he used drew a lot of online criticism, which was something Gillis seemed surprised by, considering he didn’t think his monologue was controversial. During his appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience, he said he told SNL the following about his monologue:

Fellas, I'm giving you a solid C-minus of a monologue, but I promise there's no controversy.

He confirmed that SNL never screened his monologue and trusted Gillis’s judgment. He also followed up, saying that he personally didn’t have an actual problem with the way women dress at the gym, saying:

For the record, [I] don’t have a problem with it.

Rogan questioned whether or not the clothing was appropriate and sexualized, and Gillis noted that many men are doing the same thing. However, he was admittedly upset about the online reaction and said it had an impact on his mental health. Gillis said he deleted social media as a result, as the situation spiked his cortisol levels, and he didn’t have a desire to hear what else people were saying about him.

He clearly is feeling some sort of way about the intensity of the backlash, especially when it came to other comics coming out against him -- even Michael Che joked he was sick of talking about it. However, Gillis seems to understand why the joke got so much heat. The timing of this certainly did not work in his favor, especially considering it happened while many news stories had recently broken about sexual impropriety towards women. Upon reflection, he seemed to see how the context was a big problem. He said:

I think it obviously had a lot to do with the climate.

While he wasn’t apologetic about it, he seems to understand where the anger came from. Whether his explanation changes anyone's opinion of the monologue remains to be seen.

You can revisit Shane Gillis’s SNL episode, as well as other episodes, now with a Peacock subscription. You can also check out upcoming episodes on Saturdays at 11:30 on NBC. SNL has a lot of exciting hosts and musical guests coming up for season 52, so make sure to check it out.

Pearl Abyss apologized for the presence of AI-generated art in Crimson Desert earlier this year, but it's not slowing down.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earlier this year, Pearl Abyss apologized for the presence of AI-generated art in Crimson Desert—not because it had used generative AI, mind, but because players saw it. And it seems like the odds we might see more of it in the future are going up, as the studio said in its Q3 2026 earnings letter (via Eurogamer) that it will be going even deeper on AI-powered development in the future.

The first reference to AI comes midway through the letter: "While we previously validated game systems only after implementing them manually, we now utilize AI to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," it states. "This enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed."

The studio immediately clarified, though, that AI "serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity," and that gameplay and content development "remain fully driven by our development team."

The future will see more of the same, with the same caveats. "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality," Pearl Abyss writes. "AI is being utilized across various stages of development—including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization—and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline.

"We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously."

That essentially repeats what Pearl Abyss said in February when players discovered the presence of generative AI art in Crimson Desert: It acknowledged that "some 2D visual props" had been created by AI during the early stages of development, but said they were supposed to be replaced "following final work and review by our art and development teams, with work that aligned with our quality standards and creative direction."

The studio also admitted that it had not "clearly disclosed our use of AI" in the development process, and promised to be more transparent about it in the future. This letter certainly could be seen as a step in that direction.

#3762. Crusader Kings publishers Paradox announce CEO swap, say they're "in a strong position at a time when much of the industry is facing major challenges"

"My plan was never to be CEO for life", says man clearly not embracing the grand strategy despot spirit

Paradox Interactive, publishers of umpteen strategy genre stalwarts including Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis, and Hearts of Iron, have announced plans to switch overlords early next year. Fredrik Wester will make way for Mattias Lilja, as the deputy CEO takes the throne.

While the move's been announced this week, Lilja will properly become boss from January 4th, making this a case of getting a new figurehead in place as the calendars swap. Departing CEO Fredrik Wester isn't going far, at least for now, as he'll "continue focusing on the company's long-term development as a member of the board".

"My plan was never to be CEO for life," Wester said. "The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company’s journey. Since I returned as CEO, we’ve streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over."

"The Board wants to thank Fredrik for his visionary leadership and outstanding contributions over these years," stated chairman Håkan Sjunnesson. "As a result, Paradox is in a strong position at a time when much of the industry is facing major challenges." He added that Lilja is "more than ready to assume the role and lead Paradox towards new gaming experiences that last for decades".

Lilja himself declared that Paradox have "a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games" and will be "stepping up the pace". "We will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus," he said.

As Wester alluded to, he previously served as Paradox CEO from 2009 to 2018, with a brief stint as executive chairman of the board sandwiched between that and his latest stint as CEO since 2021. Lilja has been deputy CEO since 2024 and chief of staff since 2021, having originally joined Paradox as a producer in 2009.

The past half decade has been a very mixed bag for Paradox. Their big strategy flagships keep ticking along, albeit with the question of whether their next DLC will feel worth it hovering overhead near-permanently. Outside of that, however, the likes of Cities: Skylines 2, Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines 2, and cancelled Sims competitor Life By You have made for a track record heavy on questionable decisions and games which either flopped hard or failed to blow away expectations. Wester acknowledged back in 2024 that the company had "made the wrong calls in several projects, especially outside of our core".

With the likes of post-apocalyptic strategy game Afterworld currently in the works, it'll be interesting to see if Lilja's tenure can see Paradox finally start to nail not just their nerdy bread and butter, but also games that don't involve staring down at a big map.

#3761. GTA 6 pre-orders are tracking "well above expectations" and the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two, says CEO Strauss Zelnick

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick noted that pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking "far above expectations", and is certain that soon "numbers will speak for themselves" when it comes to the game.

Zelnick also promised GTA Online and GTA 5 will continue to receive updates in order to support the "nearly 235 million" units sold to date across "an unprecedented three console generations". The GTA series as a whole has, to date, sold over 480 million units. Karl Statoff, president at Take-Two, adds the launch of GTA 6 will be a "defining moment for the company and global entertainment industry". Zelnick adds, later in a question and answer session, that he expects GTA 6 to "set a new baseline" for Take-Two. "The future's really bright across the board," he notes.

For the next quarter, Take-Two expects to deliver $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion - with "recurrent consumer spending" to raise by 12 percent, driven by "the groundbreaking release" of Grand Theft Auto 6, and expects to see "significant growth for the Grand Theft Auto series", driven by sales of - specifically - Grand Theft Auto 6's Ultimate Edition, which includes add-on content, and that most people are pre-ordering at its $100 price point. That bonus $20 between the $80 base edition and the Ultimate Edition is counted as "recurrent consumer spending", as is part of that massive bump the company has seen.

It also seems that we will see more GTA games - or content, at least - sooner than expected. "We do think that the nature and velocity of the content we'll see from our iconic franchises, including GTA, will look dramatically different over the next decade." It's a vague comment, but assumedly the work done on the engine and backend of GTA 6 means we'll see more content arriving in shorter order than we're used to for the series. This is per an article published by IGN in line with the earning's call going live.

Elsewhere in the earnings call, Take-Two referred to its current setup with its mobile, sports, 'core new IP' and 'core existing IP' as "the strongest development pipeline in the company's history". In terms of new IP, Zelnick directed investors to consider the launches of incoming projects like Ken Levine's mysterious Judas and Project Ethos (which we don't know too much about yet, other than it's billed as a "roguelike hero shooter"). For core IP, 8 sequels and 7 remakes, remasters, and platform extensions.

Buoyed by these plans, Zelnick outlines that he believes that fiscal year 2027 "will be a historic year for Take-Two" as the company is buoyed by "recent and upcoming releases". No prizes for what that's referring to. If you're curious about what sort of numbers we may be looking at here, all you need to do is cast your mind back to 2014, where you will remember GTA 5 made $1bn in just three days.

It’s sometimes hard to say what a viewer might see when they turn on their local news. You might see Tom Hiddleston blame Thor for bad weather or Zendaya and her mother in random b-roll. Anyone who was tuning into Oregon’s KVAL News at the end of this past week saw a hilarious interview involving actors Daniel Kaluuya and Tyriq Withers. The two actors were stopped and asked for their thoughts on the FAA’s flight stoppages and, now, the Internet is having a ball while reacting to the now-viral chat.

Travelers experienced an uncertain situation on Friday, November 13 when the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) grounded flights across the country. The massive move stemmed from radar and communications issues that reportedly plagued air traffic control centers. As a result, countless flights were delayed, leaving many – from everyday people to professional sports teams – stranded. As of this writing, however, the FAA has officially lifted the grounding, though delays remain.

Ahead of the FAA allowing flights to continue, though, KVAL News caught up with Withers and Kaluuya at Eugene Airport, where they had to de-board on their way to California. The interview started off normal enough, though the chat took a humorous turn when Withers channeled the “Bella Noche’” meme live on the air after reporter Gold Meadows asked him about the delays. His comment had Oscar winner Kaluuya cracking up, and I dare you not to laugh when you see the moment in the clip below:

Tyriq Withers & Daniel Kaluuya had to de-board back in Eugene, Oregon, after flights were grounded today https://t.co/SyoQOOggTSNovember 14, 2026

The Him star saw an opportunity and took his shot – and I’m so glad he did. I can’t stop watching this clip, as it’s just too perfect. Just to provide a bit of context, the original clip was footage from a WBRZ interview conducted in July 2015 in the aftermath of a shooting at the Bella Noche’ nightclub in Louisiana. People seem to love seeing him and Kaluuya together in the clip. Take a look at some of the responses that have appeared on X:

What’s particularly funny to me is just how perfectly Tyriq Withers manages to sell that line. I mean, he perfectly nails the delivery in a way that echoes the original 2015 clip. Anyone in need of evidence on that front need only to check out this comparison video:

I saw Tyriq Withers and Daniel Kaaluya at the airport being interviewed 😩🤭🤣🤣🤣 https://t.co/TYorpeVxeyNovember 14, 2026

I also think that one user was on to something when mentioning a “buddy movie,” because I’d surely watch a comedy starring Kaluuya and Withers after that viral display of hilarity. Alas, that’s just a fantasy at this point, though the two actors have remained busy amid the 2026 movie schedule in other respects. This year, Withers co-led the romance film Reminders of Him, while Kaluuya co-starred in the Chris Rock-helmed dramedy Misty Green. Both actors also have other projects in the works, and that includes Kaluuya’s Spider-Punk film.

After this viral interview, I’d imagine that a number of people wouldn’t mind seeing Daniel Kaluuya and Tyriq Withers headline a comedy together. The chances of that happening may be slim but, at the very least, we’ll always have this local news report to refer back to. Here’s hoping Withers’ comment becomes a meme in its own right.

Here are the 5 ways the DC Universe can continue in a post-James Gunn world

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nobody outside of the newly formed Skydance could have foreseen that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be out as the heads of DC Studios this early. The dynamic duo only took control four years ago, wiping the slate (almost) clean as they rebooted the franchise and set about forging a new shared universe.

Yet, here we are. Gunn and Safran are no longer DC chiefs (despite David Ellison naming them as the franchise’s continued caretakers last month), and Jeremy Latcham, best known for his work on the first stages of the Marvel Cinematic Universe alongside Kevin Feige, is now at the helm. What does that mean for Superman’s future on the big screen? It’s not entirely clear, but there are a few directions Latcham could take the DC Universe.

Below you'll find our theories on the five potential paths for DC heading forward now that all those best-laid plans for DCU Chapter One are out the window. Before we wildly speculate, you might also want to refamiliarize yourself with all the upcoming DC movies and TV shows that were previously announced.

The Gunn/Safran regime released three movies, and two of them – Superman and Clayface – were widely embraced (the less said about Supergirl, the better; even Gunn failed to mention the movie in his departing message). On the TV side, Peacemaker, Lanterns, and Creature Commandos all scored well with critics, and reports indicate 19 million people watched HBO’s Lanterns. In other words, there’s a lot of goodwill towards Gunn and Safran’s universe, and their fingerprints remain all over DC’s upcoming output, namely the Gunn-directed Man of Tomorrow, set to release next year.

However, something’s obviously not working; otherwise Gunn and Safran would still be in the job. Latcham could very well continue with the characters of Gunn’s universe, but instead of spotlighting side characters like Clayface, he could refocus the franchise on its big hitters – Batman, Wonder Woman, Aquaman, etc – and have them cross over with David Corenswet’s Superman in Justice League. This was surely Gunn’s plan to some degree (reports indicate a third Superman movie would have started to bring the pieces together), but Latcham might push to get there a little sooner. It’s also worth noting that Latcham has a history with Gunn, having executive produced Guardians of the Galaxy, so he’s a known fan of the director-turned-DC-chief-turned-director’s work.

Of course, there’s a bat-shaped shadow looming over any conversation about the future of the DC Universe. Robert Pattinson is cinema’s current incarnation of the Caped Crusader and is set to return in The Batman 2. Despite Gunn previously saying that he would introduce a new Batman in the previously announced The Brave and the Bold, many people believe that having a new Bats alongside Battinson would be both confusing for general audiences and potentially overexpose Bruce Wayne.

So, what’s Latcham to do? He could fully commit to director Matt Reeves’ version of Gotham and center the entire cinematic universe on it. After all, The Batman was hugely successful at the box office – more so than Superman – and Reeves has proven himself a deft hand at expanding the universe with The Penguin. Latcham could revive the previously dead spin-off series about the Gotham City Police Department, and potentially revisit previously pitched series based around Catwoman and Poison Ivy. He could then start broadening out the universe to add non-Batman characters, gradually building an entirely new DC Universe.

Rather than simply build out from The Batman, a relatively clean way to handle things might be to merge Gunn with Reeves’ universes. These are popular incarnations of Superman and Batman, and both have sequels coming to cinemas soon (plus Wonder Woman might be in Man of Tomorrow, if Adria Arjona is playing the character). Why not smash them all together in a new Justice League?

The biggest issue would be deciding whether a team-up movie would have Superman’s warm tone or The Batman’s cold one. Actually, that’s not quite the biggest issue: the practicalities of getting Robert Pattinson, plus his castmates Scarlett Johansson, Sebastian Stan, and Colin Farrell, to sign up for another decade of movies is another.

For Latcham, all three scenarios carry baggage. Continuing either the Gunn-verse or Battinson-verse (or both!) would mean sticking to foundations built by someone else, and these may not align with Latcham’s own vision. In fact, despite Gunn’s farewell message stating that his characters will live on, other reports have signalled that Latcham will “dismantle” the DC Universe as we know it.

If that holds, the producer could very well be looking to recast Batman and Superman, which would mean introducing a third distinct version of both superheroes in just over a decade (not to mention multiple other versions that cropped up in The Flash). If Latcham were to kickstart an all-new, fresh-faced DC Universe, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see him hard-launch with a Justice League movie: just ignore everything else – we’ve seen everyone’s origin stories too recently for a do-over – and get straight to the main event.

Frankly, very few people want to see the DC Universe rebooted so soon after the last restart. Instead, a sharpening of the current franchise’s direction, with Latcham prioritising a new Justice League movie with Corenswet’s Superman, seems the most likely route ahead. And a friendly note to Latcham to say, maybe you could go back and firmly establish what is and isn’t canon, pruning any leftovers from the previous Snyderverse and… Wait. Snyderverse? Could it be?

It’s not going to happen. But also, the return of the Snyderverse would surely be the wildest thing to ever happen to DC, right? Ben Affleck back in the suit. Henry Cavill’s Superman facing Dwayne Johnson’s Black Adam. The hierarchy of power changing!

News of Gunn and Safran leaving DC Studios has some fans tweeting out for Latcham to #RestoreTheSnyderVerse. However, Zack Snyder’s Justice League was a success on streaming, but not a colossal one – certainly not enough to justify continuing its story. There’s little chance of anything Snyder-related returning, but as Wonder Woman herself, Gal Gadot, once sang during our pandemic pandemonium: “Imagine”. The Bat-Ball’s in your court, Latcham.

Man of Tomorrow releases in theaters on July 9, 2027. While we wait, check out one writer's thoughts on why James Gunn’s brave and bold vision for the DCU deserved better than an early grave.

#3758. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

Hopefully, this results in me saying "I knew it, I knew her."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taylor Swift is doing something monumental: She’s going to perform at the CMAs for the first time in 13 years on November 18. Seriously, she’s actually going to sing at an award show airing on the 2026 TV schedule. So, obviously this got me thinking about other things that could happen during this appearance, and I have two wild theories.

Now, my logical brain sees this appearance as an opportunity for Taylor Swift’s Oscar campaign to continue. “I Knew It, I Knew You” is a country song featured in Toy Story 5, and it's nominated for Single of the Year at the CMAs. Also, Toy Story 5 is a movie you can now stream with a Disney+ subscription, the CMA Awards will air on ABC and Disney+, oh, and the Oscars will air on ABC in March. So, this feels kind of kismet.

However, you better believe my clowning Swiftie brain has some wilder theories about what could happen. And considering the unexpected things Taylor Swift has done at award shows in the past (like announcing Midnights at the VMAs and The Tortured Poets Department at the Grammys), I wouldn’t rule these far-fetched ideas out.

Now, there have been numerous (and wrong) theories about when Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version) might be announced. So, take this with a grain of salt. However, I feel like it’d be fitting for the "Our Song" singer to announce the re-recording of her debut album at the Country Music Association Awards.

Think about it: she got her start in country music, she hasn’t performed at the CMAs in 13 years (which is her favorite number), and her first album is celebrating its 20th anniversary this year. If she was going to finally give us Taylor’s Version of Debut – which she said would happen eventually after she got her music back – now feels like the time to do it.

Then there’s the idea of Taylor Swift’ 13th album. It feels like it's been looming over us, and there are theories that she might go country for this monumental project. So, announcing it at the CMAs would be appropriate.

Then, there’s the numerology of it all. Famously, the “You Need To Calm Down” singer loves her numbers, so, as @stillgotscars posted on X:

Of course, Taylor ‘I love numerology’ Swift waited until Friday the 13th to announce that she will be performing at the CMAs because it just so happens to have been 13 years since her last performance at the ceremony in 2013. Of course she did.

I just feel like all those 13s are trying to tell us something, and maybe it’s TS13.

Overall, I really think anything could happen at the CMAs. It’s been a very, very long time since Taylor Swift performed there (or at any award show, for that matter), so I feel like she has something big up her sleeve. Plus, with her history of surprising fans, we really should expect the unexpected here.

With that said, to see if any of this actually happens, you can see Taylor Swift perform at the CMA Awards on November 18 at 8 p.m. ET on ABC and Disney+.

#3756. Worst Class Ever takes asymmetrical multiplayer back to school, with a teacher player trying to spot the naughty children among the NPCs

Master the sinful art of eating sweets behind your textbook

What's the best prank you ever pulled on a teacher in school, assuming you went to school? By which I mean, a genuinely funny prank that didn't cause any injuries, break any of the more important laws (legal or ethical), or leave anybody with years of mental distress.

I'll start: I once had to write a four-page punishment essay with the topic "silence is golden", after being caught talking in class. I took the essay very seriously for the first three pages, only to end it with the phrase "...but not as golden as my arse." The teacher who set me the essay smugly tore it up without reading it - as I knew he would. Checkmate, Mr Thompson. Decades later, the last laugh remains mine.

Worst Class Ever is a new don't-call-it-friendslop asymmetrical multiplayer game dedicated to such larks. One player is a teacher, and seven others are naughty delinquent children, hiding in amongst some well-brought-up and obedient NPCs. As the wayward tykes, your goal is to do mischievous things like eating at your desk, passing notes, dropping banana skins, and playing on your phone, without being spotted by Teach.

All of this takes place in a breezy modern Japanese high school, the kind familiar from a million animes. Bagsy the Protagonist Desk by the window at the back of the class! The maplist spans the curriculum, from computer labs to gym tracks to stepped lecture theatres. I don't think there are any covert edu-tainment mechanics, but if you're playing Teacher, I guess there's nothing to stop you actually explaining the periodic table while trying to work out who keeps throwing chalk at your head.

What a wholesome and whimsical place! Such happy memories! Oh crikey, the male teacher is terrifying – why can't he stop grinning? And why do I have a smoke grenade? Why is this lesson taking place in the dark? Why are the teachers permitted to punch the students and tie them to wooden posts? Worst Class Ever definitely isn't a horror game, but I'm not sure I'd send my kids to this particular institution. I feel like we're one texture pack away from playing a more sociable version of Little Nightmares. Read more on Steam.

Roundabouts, merchant republics, and dark fantasy roguelikes aren't budging their release plans.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Though it might seem hard to believe given its inescapability, not everyone is going to be playing GTA 6 next week. Some might be waiting for its eventual PC release (whenever that ends up being). Others might simply be unwilling to spend over a thousand dollars on a console just to enjoy the privilege.

Most publishers and developers releasing a videogame this season, however, have opted to vacate the GTA 6 blast radius—but not all of them. If you're looking for something new to play next week, you'll be pleased to know there are some brave games still launching on Steam. Here are some options to consider if you aren't dropping into Vice City:

If you're a CK3 player—and you should be; it's number eight on our Top 100 list for a reason—then Paradox's next expansion should be on your radar. While everyone else is focused on Grand Theft Auto, you could be engaging in the grandest theft of all: Commerce.

Silk and Silver is all about mercantilism: Merchant families can jockey for trade route monopolies and use their wealth to lobby for influence, while new Republic governments offer patrician dynasties a venue to vie for dominance in the constitutional Assembly—potentially forming commercial or military pacts with other Republics. It's also got a lot of Italian content in it. Everyone loves Italian content.

Crusader Kings 3: Silk and Silver launches on November 17.

Among the cozier offerings arriving on Steam during GTA 6 week, Spirit Crossing is a building, crafting, and decorating MMO set in a world seemingly populated entirely by art students and befriendable spirits.

Borrowing a page from Sky: Children of the Light, it's only as much of an MMO as you want it to be: other players are only fully visible in your world if you mutually choose to engage with one another. Otherwise, you're free to roam its pastel soulscape and build out your own little corner of paradise solo for as long as you prefer.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Listen. I know. It's 2026. I feel the same suspicions that you do when you see a game with full-on pixel illustrations like this on Steam nowadays. But the developers of Harma insist that it's "developed entirely by human creators and does not contain any contents or assets generated by AI tools." Which is good, because it looks neat, and I want to believe.

It's a roguelike deckbuilder that has both a story-driven campaign and a replayable "Dimensional Rift" mode, which should provide plenty of opportunity to continue admiring the work of its pixel artists. Assuming there were, in fact, pixel artists. They wouldn't lie to me, right? Please?

Harma launches in early access on November 16.

Melvor Idle is for one of the most particular types of guys, and whether or not you're one of them should be clarified as soon as I say this sentence: Melvor Idle 2 is like Old School RuneScape with all the parts that aren't a skill grind stripped away. It's 100% gathering items so you can get better at gathering items so you can gather better items. It's pure, uncut clicking and waiting as numbers go up.

It's so thoroughly for RuneScape guys that, after the success of the first Melvor Idle, Jagex brought the operation under its publishing wing. If that's for you, I'm not judging. In many ways, you're living a more honest life than I am.

Melvor Idle 2 launches in early access on November 17.

If you do not yet acknowledge the awesome power of the roundabout, it is time to learn. Trafficity is a game about traffic. There are cars, and they must go places. But only so many cars can go to one place at once.

This is the crux on which our world is both built and broken.

And now it is yours to solve—using a toolkit of gridless road design tools, fully-customizable traffic lights, and dynamic interchange simulation. Somewhere, in another game, your uncouth lessers are disrupting this great task with the stealing and crashing of your vehicular charges. But now, you answer to a higher calling. The traffic must flow.

Publisher Devolver Digital is taking Grand Theft Auto 6 on directly with this fake remake (re-fake?) of an "unreleased" platformer starring its bizarre mascot, Volvy. Titled Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed, the game challenges players to traverse four zany platforming worlds, using Volvy's grotesquely swollen hand to smash enemies, punch through blocks, and fist-i-copter across gaps.

While Volvy's Adventure boils down to a playable joke, it is a pretty stylish one. Developer doinksoft has clearly put a lot of care into the game's crisp retro pixel art, while the platforming seems to have a decent amount of physicality to it. The game will release on the same day as Grand Theft Auto six at a discounted price, so it'll be interesting to see whether it can cut through the noise of Vice City's hyper-real traffic.

Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed launches on November 19.

#3754. Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

After Claude blocked users from "recreating someone else's specific game"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the lead up to GTA 6's long-awaited launch, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has called out companies like Anthropic and OpenAI for allowing users to plagiarize and clone pre-existing games using generative AI.

Generative AI's usage in game development has been highly controversial for many reasons, but in recent months, AI copycats have become an increasingly prevalent issue. Some Steam developers even cancelled demos or playtests out of fear their games would be cloned and put up for sale before their official release dates. Copycats of popular games like Mecca Chameleon can sometimes flood the storefront in no time, too.

"I think all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's," Zelnick says when asked if he'd like to see more AI companies restrict users from reverse engineering games, in an interview with IGN.

"And if you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected," he adds.

Anthropic recently added a new rule to Claude's backend code to block users from "recreating someone else's specific game," after lots of developers essentially had their work ripped off in mere minutes. The restriction might also stop Claude from being used in the tidal wave of vibe-coded recompilations we've seen in recent months - Mario Kart Wii, Banjo-Tooie and The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening included.

"Using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic's member of technical staff Addy Osmani said at the time. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working."

ChatGPT owner OpenAI seemingly has no such restrictions in place for now.

Could a remade Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time be exciting enough to revitalise Switch 2 hardware sales? That was the big question. And early sales figures suggest the answer is yes, it can.

The Switch 2, which had been declining in hardware sales over the last few months, just had its highest (dollar) sales week of 2026 in the US so far following the game's release, according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella on Bluesky.

The accompanying Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console in particular is responsible for a notable jump in Switch 2 hardware dollar sales. The themed, special edition console has been popular, with various retailers immediately running out of stock and a rise in scalping.

It's worth noting that The Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console, priced $520 / £430, does not include a copy of the game. Also, because the console was released 29th October, and the Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November, their sales results will come in separate monthly reports.

The Ocarina of Time launch also caused US hardware spending to jump by 81 percent during the week ending 31st October compared to the same period last year.

Christian Donlan awarded The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time a glitzy five stars in Eurogamer's review, writing: "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

#3751. While soulslikes went bigger than big, Death's Door swung open the appeal of a tighter adventure

Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones. Elden Rings and Silksongs, with vast kingdoms and deep, rattling toolkits for surviving them. The reason it’s a fool’s game is because you can also have something like Death’s Door, a taut, compact, lighthearted little actioner that fills eight hours instead of 80 and yet never feels underwhelming or compromised for it.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition. You are a crow. You hit things. Occasionally you shoot things. You collect the souls of a frog, a yeti, and a grandmother. Everything in-between directly relates to finding the errant monster/pensioner, or at a stretch, upgrading one of those four abilities.

Still, it’s clever with its limitations. Environments are small in number but vary wildly in tone and texture, and they tightly weave their paths into criss-crossing bundles that maximise travel – evoking the sense of a great, ranging adventure within relatively tiny spaces. The lack of a wiki’s worth of combat options also never becomes a problem, partly because it spreads out its spell unlocks, and partly because the smooth, flowing back-and-forths of its central swordplay are pleasurable enough to carry it anyway. Good bosses, too! They’re all characterful, memorable weirdoes who fight unlike anyone in their minion armies, and usually come with a hidden weakness to deduce and exploit.

Which is welcome, as these big lads and lasses do tend to launch difficulty spikes right up your feathered backside, and do so in a game that isn’t otherwise as fussed about trial-and-error pain endurance as some of its inspirations. They don’t, however, bring the mood down. At times, this tale of a pitch-black soul reaper working as an agent of Death (complete with an office of Death and embittered co-workers of Death) can get downright cosy, leading through you through warmly-lit jungles and breezy waterside ruins.

Recently replaying, I’d also forgotten how witty it can be. Little gaglets are sprinkled throughout, both visual and verbal, but the best jokes are saved for – funnily enough – the bosses, who’ll raise your pre-fight spirit with some amusingly terrible trash talk before becoming the punchline themselves. I audibly wheezed the first time a death animation immediately cut to the foe’s impromptu funeral, their beaked killer among the precious few guests. And even when the joke is recycled later, I couldn’t help tittering at the sight of my enemy – who seconds earlier, had been attempting to fatally sit on me – lying nobly in state.

I previously considered ending my Valor Mortis review by calling it a gateway into the more demanding side of action-RPGs; a shorter, simpler alternative to FromSoft’s overwhelming titans that might nonetheless serve to introduce curious newcomers to their shared quirks and qualities. The game equivalent of splashing your chest with water before jumping into a pool. In hindsight, Death’s Door was always a better fit for that description, though there’s enough else here you don’t need to be prepping for something tougher to appreciate its lean, keen adventuring.

Nothing prepared me for Andrea Riseborough and Tramell Tillman's transformations either.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I remember the first time I saw Johnny Depp’s Ebenezer Scrooge, and I recall being both terrified and in awe. Now, as Ti West’s take on A Christmas Carol premieres on the 2026 movie schedule, I got to speak to Depp’s co-stars about his transformation and their own. Sam Claflin specifically told me why nothing prepared him for what he saw when the lead of Ebenezer showed up on set. Meanwhile, his co-stars who play the ghosts proved why their looks were just as remarkable.

When it comes to Ebenezer, one of the primary talking points has been Johnny Depp’s transformation. He’s almost unrecognizable as the old Scrooge, and his performance in the movie is something to behold (whether you love it or not). When I asked Sam Claflin, who plays Fred in the film, about seeing his co-star in character for the first time, he made it clear it was intense, as he explained:

Terrifying. I had seen an image. I'd seen an early image. Ti had shown me an image of Johnny, like a makeup test. You know, with all the prosthetics on. It's sort of that, but it's also the physicality that he brought. The way that he'd shuffle in the voice and the funny little laugh, like he completely disappears within every role that he does, and this is no exception. Terrifying.

The Catching Fire actor went on to call the makeover “remarkable,” and he made it clear he’s “in awe” of actors who “completely transform themselves.” Explaining that point further, he said:

It's sort of remarkable, and honestly, I'm in awe. I'm in awe of actors like that, like the Christian Bales of the world, the people that just completely transform themselves, and are unafraid and unapologetic and just bold, bold with their choices. And it was terrifying the first time.

I also have to note that when I asked Claflin what it’s like to be the recipient of one of Johnny Depp’s bah humbugs, he made a similar point. He noted that when it happened, it shook him, and he couldn’t get the image of the actor out of his head:

I think seeing him in character still shakes me to my core. I mean, I can't get the image out of my head. But you know, he's just so funny, like with the character, but also obviously in between takes and stuff. Yeah, he just sort of brought so much levity to the film set, but to the experience and to the film itself. Yeah, it was a joy to be a part of anything that he's a part of.

Now, Depp’s Ebenezer is something. However, I do think it’s important to note that he was not the only actor in this film who went through a massive and jaw-dropping transformation.

Alongside Depp and Claflin, Ebenezer also features Tramell Tillman and Andrea Riseborough as the Ghosts of Christmas Present and Past, respectively. Like the man who plays the titular character, they’re both almost unrecognizable in their parts, and the process of looking like that was not for the faint of heart, as they told me:

In Riseborough’s case, she had to turn fully white, as she took on the Ghost of Christmas Past. She also wore white contacts, which she told me was one of the tougher parts of the transformation because it was hard to see through them. Tillman agreed, saying eyesight was the “biggest challenge” he faced in terms of his character's look. However, along with the contacts, he was covered in makeup and prosthetics that made him look like he was decaying.

They both looked incredible, and much like Claflin’s reaction to seeing Depp for the first time, I was both terrified and in awe of these ghosts.

Now, Ebenezer has not gotten the best reviews. However, there’s no denying the transformations the actors went through for it are remarkable. So, you can be the judge of whether you like this take on A Christmas Carol or not by catching Ebenezer in theaters now.

#3749. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is getting three big updates with new starting scenarios - organ trading, junk empires and fine dining

Mucky and disreputable kiosk game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim is getting three big updates over the next few months that add extra starting scenarios, building on the existing wealth of goods, materials, vocations and techs. Those starting scenarios range from peddling human meat to running the finest cyber-frappucino stall this side of Tannhäuser Gate. There are no hard release dates, and the contents of each update may alter, but developers Questing Goose Studio have shared some rough timeframes.

Coming up in mid-December, there's the Junker starting scenario, which I assume is all about trading scrap, rather than being a Prussian nobleman. You'll get a bespoke perk, new items, and the ability to hire, equip and send scavs on expeditions. This update will also include some minor expansions for the Fence and Gunsmith vocations – the latter will be able to flog or otherwise make use of shotgun shells, 25mm grenade rounds and a tier 3 handmade SMG, alongside new armour.

Late January is when you'll "very likely" get the chance to be an Organ Dealer, care of the second major update. "Players will start by buying different organs and fulfilling specific requests, and will later be able to grow or print organs," a Steam blog explains. You'll also be able to filter blood and remove diseases, with different blood types having different value modifiers. How will you get your hands on organs? By sending horrible black market thugs on foraging "expeditions".

Last but not least, the planned April update will add the Street Food Vendor starting scenario. This lets you weave a livelihood around choice beverages and edibles from a range of cultures, supported by updates to the game's Aquaculture and Hydroponics tech. Sounds a lot cheerier than the organ trading racket, but then again, Probably Stolen will doubtless find a way to make it utterly grim. Guests at Sweeney's Cantina know better than to ask what our frappucinos are made of.

Are you playing Probably Stolen? It's been doing better than expected. I was keen on the demo, but my attention was lured away by a truly upsetting game about dogpeople in caves.

"We penalised shooting so much in that game," says design director Jens Andersson.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Indiana Jones and The Great Circle offered such a great depiction of everyone's favourite Nazi-thumping archaeologist that it's hard to imagine developer MachineGames building that game any differently. Yet according to design director Jens Andersson, getting the Indy feel of The Great Circle right represented a significant challenge for the Swedish studio.

One of the hardest problems MachineGames struggled with was the presence of guns—specifically, how to stop players from just blasting through armies of Nazis without making guns less fun to use. Speaking to FRVR, Andersson explained that having satisfying firearms in The Great Circle was "non-negotiable" as "we have a lot of people at Machine[Games] that love guns".

Since MachineGames wanted The Great Circle to be true to Spielberg's films, they needed guns to be a part of Indy's toolset but not the default response to every problem. One partial solution was to make reloading slow, encouraging players to use other tools like Indy's whip or his fists, but this alone wasn't enough.

"We had so many designs to try and get around that," Andersson continued. "For example, a GTA star level system when you shoot someone and reinforcements [start] coming in." The thinking here seems to have been to discourage players from going overboard with loud weapons. "Because we were so afraid that this would be the default thing that the player would do. They take down a guy, they see a gun on the floor, and they clear the whole area with just guns."

In the end, the solution MachineGames stumbled on was to provide alternative, breakable melee weapons ranging from frying pans to violins. These abundant, lightly comedic tools encouraged players to embrace the improvisational nature of how Indy fights, offering a quick knockout both in stealth and when the player's ammunition ran dry.

Remarkably, Andersson says that breakable weapons "got in very late" during development. But when the studio "saw how effective it was, that's when we started putting all this weird stuff in. The violin, all of this weird stuff that makes it a little slapstick-y, but not slapstick."

This system proved instrumental in getting the final balance of Indy's combat right, where stealth and fisticuffs are the primary approach, while guns tend to be a last resort. "We penalised shooting so much in that game. I know a lot of people are frustrated about that, but many more people love it," Andersson says. "The thing that really fixed it was that we made melee combat so interesting, fun, and easy. Not easy challenge-wise, but just it's easy to get into. You stealth up, you hit someone from behind, the breakable weapon system was super important to do that. 'Oh, there's a new weapon, it's a fly swatter, I want to try this.'"

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Ultimately, Indy's dynamic combat was a big part of what made it Machine Games' best game to date, earning it a score of 86 in PC Gamer's Indiana Jones and the Great Circle Review. Whether we'll see another Indy game from Machine Games is still up in the air. But if it does happen, it probably won't be soon, as the studio has just confirmed that's it's working on Wolfenstein 3.
